lesson.title: Writing a List Straight to Disk: The writelines() Method
lesson.summary: The writelines() method writes every string in a list, or any iterable of strings, to a file one after another without inserting newlines between them, so each string needs its own trailing newline if separate lines are what you want.
lesson.body:
`writelines()` is to `write()` what `readlines()` is to `read()`, but the naming is a little misleading, so it is worth being precise about what it actually does. `file.writelines(some_list)` takes a list, or really any iterable, of strings and writes each one to the file in order, one right after another. What it does not do, despite the name, is add a newline character between them. If the strings in the list do not already end with `"\n"`, `writelines()` will not add one, and everything will run together on a single line.

```python
lines = ["Roses are red\n", "Violets are blue\n", "Python is fun\n"]

file = open("poem2.txt", "w")
file.writelines(lines)
file.close()

file = open("poem2.txt", "r")
print(file.read())
file.close()
```

```python
Roses are red
Violets are blue
Python is fun
```

Because each string in `lines` already carries its own trailing `"\n"`, `writelines()` produces a file that looks exactly like three separate lines, and reading it back with `read()` confirms it, with the familiar extra blank line at the end coming from `print()` adding its own newline after content that already ended in one, the same pattern you saw with `readlines()`. This pairing is useful in practice: `readlines()` gives you a list of lines you can edit, filter, or sort, and `writelines()` is how you save that edited list back to disk.

```python
file = open("nolines.txt", "w")
file.writelines(["a", "b", "c"])
file.close()

file = open("nolines.txt", "r")
print(file.read())
file.close()
```

```python
abc
```

This second example shows the naming gotcha directly. None of `"a"`, `"b"`, or `"c"` contains a newline, so `writelines()` glues them together with nothing in between, producing a file that contains just `"abc"` on one line. Notice there is no blank line in this output, unlike the previous example, because the string read back does not end with a newline character at all. That confirms the blank line seen earlier was never a bug, it was `print()` adding its own newline on top of one that was already there in the data.
